741.quote_or_event: Guru Hargobind, the sixth Guru, built up a Sikh army and fortified his cities; he built a fort near Amritsar named Lohgarh, instilled the will to fight and high morale in his followers, and his Sikhs went on to defeat Shah Jahan's armies four times, adding to Sikh ideals the right and duty to defend the faith by the sword if necessary.
741.explanation: After Guru Arjan's martyrdom, Guru Hargobind gave the community both a spiritual and a temporal centre, and a fortress that served as a base for its armed defence.
741.tie_back: The Kural calls a fortress a treasure both for those who march out to fight and for those who shelter in fear; Guru Hargobind's Lohgarh was built for a community that had to do both.
741._accuracy_note: A reasonable historical parallel; Sikh teaching permits arms only in defence of the faith and the oppressed, so the Kural's picture of a fort as a base for attacking others fits only in part.

742.quote_or_event: “A fortress like that of Sri Lanka, with the ocean as a moat around it - there is no news about that house of Raavan.”
742.explanation: Bhagat Kabir recalls Ravana's island citadel, defended by the sea itself, to show that even the strongest natural defences do not last.
742.tie_back: The Kural lists clear water, open ground, hills and forest as a fortress's natural defences; Kabir names the greatest of water-moats, but only to say that it could not keep Ravana's house in being.
742.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 481, Raag Aasaa, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
742._accuracy_note: Next-best only: Kabir shares the image of water as a fortress's defence but uses it to teach impermanence and the need for the Name, the opposite of the Kural's practical praise of natural defences.

743.quote_or_event: “How can the beautiful fortress be conquered, O Siblings of Destiny? It has double walls and triple moats.”
743.explanation: Kabir pictures the ego-bound self as a fortress with double ramparts and triple moats, defended by the passions, so strong that no ordinary person can take it.
743.tie_back: The Kural defines a fort by height, breadth, strength and inaccessibility; Kabir's fortress with its double walls and triple moats has exactly those qualities, though he means the fortress of the mind.
743.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1161, Raag Bhairao, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
743._accuracy_note: Close in its picture of an impregnable wall, but allegorical: the fortress is the self ruled by maya and ego, which Kabir wants to see conquered, not defended.

744.quote_or_event: “It is defended by the five elements, the twenty-five categories, attachment, pride, jealousy and the awesomely powerful Maya. The poor mortal being does not have the strength to conquer it; what should I do now, O Lord? … The greed that fills their hearts is the arrow; with these things, their fortress is impregnable.”
744.explanation: In the same hymn Kabir describes the garrison and weapons of the fortress of maya, and confesses that its defences break the will of anyone who tries to storm it by his own strength.
744.tie_back: The Kural's fort crushes the zeal of the enemy that attacks it; Kabir's fortress so daunts the attacker that he cries he has no strength to take it.
744.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1161, Raag Bhairao, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
744._accuracy_note: Partial and allegorical: the demoralising fortress is the self's bondage to maya, and the hymn goes on to show it taken by divine love, so the sympathy runs opposite to the Kural's; nothing corresponds to the Kural's narrow perimeter and spacious interior.

745.quote_or_event: When the Rajput hill chiefs and imperial Mughal contingents laid siege to Guru Gobind Singh's fort at Anandpur, the Guru and his Sikhs withstood their successive assaults over many months despite dire scarcity of food caused by the prolonged blockade, until the besieged were reduced to desperate straits.
745.explanation: The Encyclopaedia of Sikhism shows that Anandpur held firm against assault, and that the blockade's real weapon was hunger.
745.tie_back: The Kural says a fortress must be hard to take and well stocked with food; Anandpur proved the first, and its ordeal shows why the second matters.
745.source: Encyclopaedia of Sikhism (ed. Harbans Singh, Punjabi University, Patiala), entry Gobind Singh, Guru
745._accuracy_note: A strong historical illustration, though a negative one (the fort's stores ran out), and sources differ on dating the siege to 1704 or 1705.

746.quote_or_event: At Anandpur, which Guru Gobind Singh had fortified, the Khalsa was given concrete form at the Baisakhi gathering of 1699: the Panj Piare, five Sikhs of different castes and regions, were initiated first, and the Khalsa were enjoined to succour the helpless and fight the oppressor, to have faith in one God and to consider all human beings equal.
746.explanation: Guru Gobind Singh founded a disciplined, casteless fellowship of saint-soldiers whose duty was to stand by the weak in the hour of danger.
746.tie_back: The Kural says a true fortress holds everything needed and good, brave men who help when danger comes; the Khalsa gave the fortress of Anandpur exactly such defenders.
746.source: Encyclopaedia of Sikhism (ed. Harbans Singh, Punjabi University, Patiala), entry Gobind Singh, Guru
746._accuracy_note: A reasonable fit on the human element of a fort; the Khalsa is first a spiritual order with a code of conduct, not a garrison, and the Kural's material stores are not addressed.

747.quote_or_event: After months of siege, the besiegers of Anandpur offered the Sikhs safe exit on solemn oaths; but as soon as the Guru and his Sikhs came out, the hill rulers and their Mughal allies fell upon them, and Guru Gobind Singh later rebuked Emperor Aurangzeb in his Zafarnamah for commanders who had perjured their oath and treacherously attacked him once he was outside the safety of his fortification.
747.explanation: Anandpur was not taken by blockade or assault; it was emptied by a false promise, and the betrayal is remembered as one of the defining wrongs of Sikh history.
747.tie_back: The Kural's true fortress cannot be taken by siege, by storming or by treachery; Anandpur resisted the first two and fell only to the third.
747.source: Encyclopaedia of Sikhism (ed. Harbans Singh, Punjabi University, Patiala), entry Gobind Singh, Guru
747._accuracy_note: A strong fit: the event shows siege, assault and treachery as the three ways a fort is lost; the Zafarnamah is in the Dasam Granth tradition, but here it is only cited as history through the Encyclopaedia, not quoted as scripture.

748.quote_or_event: After the evacuation of Anandpur, Guru Gobind Singh reached Chamkaur with barely forty Sikhs and his two elder sons; when the imperial army surrounded them, his sons Ajit Singh and Jujhar Singh and all but five of the Sikhs fell in the action, and the five survivors then bade the Guru save himself to reconsolidate the Khalsa.
748.explanation: A handful of Sikhs held a small walled haveli against a far larger besieging force long enough for the Guru to escape.
748.tie_back: The Kural's true fortress lets those inside, holding firm to their posts, prevail against a skilled besieging army; at Chamkaur the defenders held their ground to the death and secured what mattered most, the Guru's survival.
748.source: Encyclopaedia of Sikhism (ed. Harbans Singh, Punjabi University, Patiala), entry Gobind Singh, Guru
748._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: the defenders held firm as the Kural requires, but they did not defeat the besiegers, and the date is given as 1704 or 1705 in different sources.

749.quote_or_event: “He alone is known as a spiritual hero, who fights in defense of religion. He may be cut apart, piece by piece, but he never leaves the field of battle.”
749.explanation: In a salok in Raag Maaroo, Kabir says that true heroism is recognised on the battlefield itself, in the one who fights for the right and never abandons his post.
749.tie_back: The Kural says a fortress wins its fame from the deeds of its defenders at the very front of battle; Kabir likewise locates a warrior's renown in standing firm on the field.
749.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1105, Raag Maaroo (Salok), Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
749._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: the salok exalts the warrior who stands firm, but its field is first the inner battle against vice and the defence of the poor (as Sahib Singh reads it), and it says nothing of fortresses.

750.quote_or_event: “Millions of religious leaders failed to halt the invader, when they heard of the Emperor’s invasion. He burned the rest-houses and the ancient temples; he cut the princes limb from limb, and cast them into the dust. None of the Moguls went blind, and no one performed any miracle.”
750.explanation: Guru Nanak describes Babur's sack of the Punjab and mocks the defenders who trusted in the spells of holy men rather than in competent action; their strongholds and palaces fell all the same.
750.tie_back: The Kural says no fortress is a fortress in the hands of people who lack skill in action; Guru Nanak shows a whole realm's defences failing because its holders relied on charms instead of deeds.
750.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 417-418, Raag Aasaa (Ashtapadi, Babarvani), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
750._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: the hymn exposes defenders who lacked effective action, matching the Kural's point, but its main theme is God's will (hukam) and the folly of trusting in miracles, and it does not speak of fortresses as such.
